opening.headline: We explore how the fact that inference can be processed in a different region interacts with data residency requirements, and how to control and verify this interaction.
body: There is a requirement that data must not leave a specific region. If model invocation is processed in another region with available capacity, what happens then? Even if data storage remains in Region A, prompts and responses could be transmitted to Region B while being processed. Without understanding this architecture, one might mistakenly believe that residency requirements are being satisfied.

In this lesson, we examine what cross-region inference is, how Snowflake's four routing options, Claude platform's inference_geo, and Google Cloud's region specification each determine location. Finally, we explore a case study illustrating the trade-off that occurs when attempting to restrict processing to within the EU, resulting in a reduced availability of models.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: This can explain the relationship between cross-region inference and data residency.
Residential requirements and available models and performance can be distinguished.

screens.title: Inference can be processed in a different region.
screens.lead: Please examine how the storage location and processing location can differ by looking at the diagram. Please review the current state of the data in each of the two regions shown in the diagram.

paragraphs: One organization has data residency requirements. It requires that data not leave a specific region. The team believed they had satisfied the requirement by configuring the data to be stored within that region.

However, model invocation is different. Cross-region inference involves processing a request in another region that has available capacity. While data is stored only in the region where the account is located, prompts and responses are temporarily transferred to the processing region during inference. In this case, data is stored in Region A, but inference processing occurs in Region B.

If you do not understand this structure, you may mistakenly assume that you have verified the residency requirement by merely checking the storage location. This course covers methods for verifying and controlling where a model is executed within a region.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: Does our organization's residency requirement go beyond simply "where is the data stored?" to include "where is the data processed?" This question serves as the starting point for the entire course.

screens.outro: First, let's recall how much we know about the processing location in our current environment.

screens.title: Is the model being executed in a specific region being verified?
screens.lead: When you select a question, the instructor's thought process unfolds. Please first think through the answer mentally before clicking it in.

items.prompt: What is the default routing configuration for our account?
items.answer: Even if you don't directly modify the settings, a default value may be applied to the account. You will need to check the settings to determine what the default value is and whether it meets the residency requirements. Keep in mind that the default value might cover a broad range.

items.prompt: Is the actual processing location indicated in the response?
items.answer: Response metadata may include the processing region depending on the service. Configuration is intent, and response is the outcome. Without the habit of verifying the outcome, you won't know when configuration is misaligned.

items.prompt: Do you mean residence requirements apply only to storage, or do they also include processing?
items.answer: It differs according to the contract and regulations. If the requirement only limits storage, cross-region inference may not pose a problem; however, if the requirement also limits processing, routing scope must be strictly controlled. This distinction will serve as the basis for all subsequent judgments.

screens.title: Cross-region inference: Snowflake's four routing methods
screens.lead: Compare the routing options in the table in order from the widest to the narrowest scope, row by row. The processing scope, gains, and losses are summarized for each column.

data.caption: Processing Scope by Value of CORTEX_ENABLED_CROSS_REGION
rows: Snowflake processes data in any region or cloud it supports.
When the widest model selection, highest throughput, maximum resilience, and lowest cost are required.
`AWS_GLOBAL`, `AZURE_GLOBAL`, `GCP_GLOBAL`, or a combination separated by commas
Processed only within the designated cloud service provider.
Data must remain within a specific cloud's network, yet costs and throughput must also be considered.
Processing is restricted to the specified region within the specified cloud. Both cloud and region are limited.
When data must reside in a specific cloud network and a specific geographic location
Process only in home regions with accounts.
When strict data residency or geographic sovereignty requirements are present and no latest model is needed.
data.notes: All four are valid operational configurations, and the question is to select the one that meets the requirements. Commonly, customer data is stored only in regions where accounts exist, and prompts and responses are transmitted to processing regions only during processing and are not stored in the processing region. Communication occurs over a private backbone network within the same cloud or over the public internet between clouds, encrypted using mTLS. The most stringent `DISABLED` comes at the cost of reduced availability of models and features deployed in the home region.

screens.outro: Let's take a look at how other services handle the same issue through tabs.

screens.title: Region fixation and processing location verification: Claude platform and Google Cloud
screens.lead: Select each tab to compare Claude platform's two regional configurations with Google Cloud's region specification method.

visual.alt: A diagram showing the control of the difference between the request-level inference_geo and the workspace-level geo.
labels: Workspace geo: storage location and endpoint handling, configured at creation time, cannot be modified thereafter

tabs.label: Two settings
tabs.body: Claude platform's data residency control is composed of two independent settings. The inference geo specifies where model inference is executed on a request basis. The workspace geo defines where data is stored and where endpoint operations such as image transformation and code execution take place. The separate configuration of storage and processing directly aligns with the core distinction of this course.

tabs.label: inference_geo
tabs.body: `inference_geo` is a parameter in a `POST /v1/messages` request. Its two values are `global` (the default, allowing execution in any region according to performance and availability) and `us` (U.S. infrastructure only). At workspace level, `allowed_inference_geos` restricts permitted regions, while `default_inference_geo` specifies the region used when a request omits the parameter. Requesting a value outside the allowlist returns an API error.

tabs.label: Verify actual processing region
tabs.body: The value provided in the request is merely requested; the actual result is confirmed in the response. The response contains a `usage` object with a `inference_geo` field that indicates where inference was actually executed. For example, reading `response.usage.inference_geo` confirms whether it is `us`. In audits or reviews, the response value is a more direct piece of evidence than the settings screen.

tabs.label: Workspace geo and constraints
tabs.body: Workspace geo is set when creating a workspace and cannot be changed afterward. The only currently available value is `us`. `inference_geo` is supported starting from Claude 4.6 models; using it with earlier models results in a 400 error. US-only reasoning is calculated at 1.1 times the standard rate, and speed limits are shared across all regions. Thus, fixing a region incurs costs and trade-offs in both pricing and model selection.

tabs.label: Google Cloud
tabs.body: Google Cloud's Agent Platform stores and processes data only in the region specified by the user. Data labeling tasks and experimental or preview features are exceptions. Global locations are not supported, and to specify a region, you must use region-specific endpoints such as `europe-west4-aiplatform.googleapis.com`. Feature availability varies by region, so you must first verify whether the desired features are available in your chosen region.

screens.outro: Now let's examine the code for how to read settings and verify the processing location.

screens.title: Verification of processing location and auditable configuration
screens.lead: The following is a set of commands to query and modify cross-region settings in Snowflake. Please check the symptoms when the line numbers in the right-hand explanation do not align.

notes.note: `SHOW PARAMETERS` displays the value currently applied to the account. The `value` column shows the actual effective value. If no parameter has been set, the account inherits the default value; new organizations inherit the value from `ANY_REGION`, while other commercial accounts inherit either `AWS_US` or `AZURE_EU`, which represent regional values from the same cloud region. If residency requirements apply, do not rely on default values—explicitly set them instead.

`AWS_GLOBAL` is processed only within the cloud provider specified in the request. Since the region is not restricted, it is insufficient if residency requirements extend to geographic boundaries. In such cases, the symptom manifests as operations occurring despite a regional mismatch.

`AWS_EU,AZURE_EU`-like, values can be concatenated with commas to allow combinations of multiple clouds and regions. This approach limits both clouds and regions. As the allowed scope narrows, the available models are restricted to those deployed within that specific region.

`DISABLED` is the most strict state that is processed only within the home region. When misaligned, the symptom is a call failure. If you call a model or feature that is not deployed in the home region, it becomes unavailable.

`ANY_REGION` provides the broadest range of supported models and the highest capacity. If residency requirements are included up to the processing location, this value becomes a setting that exceeds requirements. This parameter can only be set at the account level and can only be modified by the `ACCOUNTADMIN` role.

screens.title: Commentary: Conflict of fixing the region reduces the available models
screens.lead: The instructor breaks down the European residency requirements step by step. Select the right arrow to proceed to the next step.

visual.alt: A stair-step diagram showing the tendency that as the processing scope is narrowed, the number of available models and throughput decrease.

steps.title: situation
steps.body: There is a requirement for European residents to handle European customers' data, prompting the team to restrict model inference processing within the EU. The team split into two factions: one advocating for immediately applying the most stringent settings, and the other pushing to keep the settings broad to allow access to the latest models.

steps.title: Step 1: Break down the requirements
steps.body: First, we determine whether the requirement is merely that storage be within the EU, or whether both storage and processing must be within the EU. Storage location and processing location are separate issues. If only storage is required, cross-region inference may be allowed; however, if both storage and processing are required, the routing scope must be restricted to the EU. Choosing without this distinction leads to either overly restrictive or insufficient configurations.

steps.title: Step 2: Select the setting
steps.body: If processing must occur in the EU, then region-specific values such as `AWS_EU` or `AZURE_EU`, or `DISABLED` when the home region is in the EU, narrow the scope accordingly. Cloud-specific settings (such as `AWS_GLOBAL` and others) only restrict to cloud regions without limiting geographic regions, thus failing to meet this requirement. For services like Claude whose region values are fixed, it is necessary to first verify whether the provided value includes the EU. Currently, `inference_geo` consists of two values: `us` and `global`.

steps.title: Step 3: Verify availability
steps.body: Verify that the desired models and features are actually available within the restricted scope. If you use only the home region, models and features are limited to that region, and services that specify regions may have different feature availability across regions. If the required model is not available within the specified scope, it indicates that the requirements and model are incompatible.

steps.title: Step 4: Evaluate conflicts
steps.body: Narrowing the scope may cause some models to be excluded, reduce throughput and resilience, and potentially increase pricing depending on the service. For example, U.S.-only inference on the Claude platform is charged at 1.1 times the standard rate. Latency between regions may vary depending on infrastructure conditions, so it is recommended to measure it directly in real-world use cases. Regarding costs, Snowflake charges based on consumption within the requested region, with no cross-region egress costs.

steps.title: Step 5: Decide
steps.body: If residency requirements take precedence, switch to the model provided within that scope and adjust the throughput plan if performance is insufficient. If model availability takes precedence, negotiate to redefine the requirement from processing to just storage. Regardless of the choice, record the decision with a configuration value and regularly verify the actual processing location through response metadata or configuration queries.

steps.title: result
steps.body: Residency requirements are not provided free of charge; instead, they are exchanged for portions of performance and availability. This case concludes with an explicit determination of what is obtained and what is given up.

screens.outro: Finally, let's summarize the decision criteria derived from the case.

screens.title: Residency requirements are traded off against performance and availability.
screens.lead: Let's summarize the content of this class in a coherent flow. Please read it from the perspective of distinguishing between storage location and processing location.

paragraphs: Cross-region inference refers to the approach of processing a request in another region that has the capacity to handle it. The location of data storage and the location of processing are distinct issues; merely because a storage region is appropriate does not mean that the processing region is also appropriate. We must first decompose what exactly is meant by residency requirements.

Each service has different control mechanisms. Snowflake allows selection among four levels: global, cloud-specific, region-specific, and disabled; Claude platform controls via request-level `inference_geo` and workspace-level limits; Google Cloud processes and stores data only within specified regions. A common trend is that stricter controls result in fewer available models and reduced throughput.

Configuration is not complete simply by setting it. You must verify the actual processing location through response fields or configuration queries to achieve a verifiable state. Finally, explicitly determine and document what is being provided in exchange for meeting requirements.

Going back to the opening scene, the team had initially only checked for storage and felt reassured. However, what they actually needed were two key questions: does the requirement include processing, and where is processing actually occurring right now? With answers to these two questions, one can make an informed choice between residency requirements and performance considerations.

callout.label: organizing
callout.text: Residency requirements are performance and availability trade-offs.

glossary.def: This approach processes the request in a region with available capacity rather than a region with an account.
Requirements regarding the geographic location where data is stored or processed.
This setting restricts reasoning processing to a specific region or area.
Parameter in Claude API that specifies the region where inference will be executed per request, with values being global and us.
This is a list of actually available models within the selected processing scope.

misconceptions.myth: If the storage region matches, the residency requirement is satisfied.
misconceptions.fact: Inference processing may occur in a different region. Even if data is stored only in the account region, prompts and responses may be transmitted to the processing region during processing, so the processing location must also be verified.

misconceptions.myth: Region fixation enhances security without any cost.
misconceptions.fact: Narrowing the scope reduces model selection, throughput, and resilience, and pricing varies depending on the service. For example, U.S.-only inference on the Claude platform charges 1.1 times the standard rate.

misconceptions.myth: Once configured, there is no need to separately verify the processing location.
misconceptions.fact: Configuration is intent, and response is the result. To verify actual values, you must use queries such as usage.inference_geo or SHOW PARAMETERS.

closing.lead: Summarizes the key points of this class.
points: Residency requirements are performance, availability, and interchangeability.
Storage location and processing location are different issues.
Cross-region configuration is staged from global to home region limited, and the stricter the setting, the fewer models become available.
Along with the configuration, verify the actual processing location using response metadata or configuration query.
